justifications.c1: The only money figure for the problem (£200 per trap per season of manual checking vs ~£50/yr automated) is a vendor's opinion on a test-mirror host; GWCT's £40k keeper employment cost is not apportioned to trap rounds, and no fine amounts or lost-game figures were found.
justifications.c2: Daily physical inspection of every live cage trap is a licence condition in England (GL33 via BPCA, search-confirmed) and Scotland (GWCT, COPFS, RSPCA v Shinton), twice daily where reds are present; but in England the sensor cannot legally replace the 'physical' check.
justifications.c3: Daily rounds, volunteer dispatchers and camera monitoring are documented, and a peer-reviewed study shows remote monitors cut visits 98% (search-confirmed), but no independent hours or £ cost for keeper rounds was found and the England licence wording keeps the round.
justifications.c4: General licences under WCA 1981 s.16 require daily physical inspection, with Animal Welfare Act exposure and welfare prosecutions (COPFS, magpie Larsen case); but no record submission is required and no regulator accepts remote alerts, so the rule works against the product.
justifications.c5: Head keeper job description (Hatfield House) and a retailer blog mention budget oversight; conservation groups hold grants (CWS3 £60/ha/yr; Moffat group's £490 for two sensors), but buyers are small, fragmented (~3,000 keepers) and budgets are tiny.
justifications.c6: Trap retailers already bundle remote trap tags (Perdix sells traps plus its own PerdixPro tags; a GSM/CCTV retailer sells Keepguard KG45), but Perdix is itself the competitor and no other channel (feed reps, land agents, insurers) was found.
justifications.c7: Crowded: PerdixPro tags (~€118–147; the file's €141.95 is the regular tag, not the small one), MinkPolice, Remoti, Keepguard (~€94), LTA, Vectronic TT5 satellite and Celium; only a coverage/price gap is suggested (Newcastle Univ. lab).
justifications.c8: Door-closure physics is simple and 100% reliable in field trials, but off-the-shelf LoRaWAN contacts cost £69/$65, rural 4G covers only ~50% of UK landmass from all operators (Scottish Gov FOI), so LoRaWAN gateways or satellite are needed.
justifications.c9: The incumbent model is a tag plus a small monthly fee only while trapping (seasonal, Perdix), there is no statutory record submission in England, and no subscription price was found.
justifications.c10: Enforcement (COPFS prosecution, magpie Larsen conviction), peer-reviewed research, local news (DNG24 Moffat grant), a practitioner forum thread (Stalking Directory) and parliamentary evidence, though much concerns welfare rather than the labour pain.

weakest: In England the general licence requires traps to be 'physically inspected' daily, so a sensor cannot remove the round it is meant to replace, and the market already has several £95–£150 cellular trap tags.
